messages.author: 1e3d5fb4e5e2a5e5
messages.subject: Natural selection analisys using Geometrics Morphometrics
parts:
Hello everyone!
I have some questions about phenotypic selection analysis, using geometrics morphometrics.

1- First, what possibilities does geomorph offer to carry out these analyzes? The linear models that using RRPP are very useful, but in the case of natural selection, fitness is a response variable, not the shape.

2- The papers that I have read use the PC axes as shape variables. Is there any analysis where I can directly use the coordinates of landmarks?

3- Finally, I have carried out the phenotypic selection analysis using PC axes as shape variables, which is currently the most accessible. If I am interested in predicting the shape from PCs predicted values by selection analysis, is there a way to do it in geomorph? that is, obtain selection coefficients on landmark coordinates?

Thanks!!

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Natural selection analisys using Geometrics Morphometrics
parts:
Federico,

I’m not sure if I understand completely what you are attempting to do but if you have a measure of fitness and shape variables, you can ask if they are associated with a two-block PLS analysis (two.b.pls in geomorph).  PLS is more like a correlation analysis than a linear model analysis.  You could use PCs of shape as independent variables in a linear model, but I’m not sure what value the coefficients are, as the PCs are not real variables (that independently mean something) but are summary axis of shape variation.  Collectively you might ascertain that the PCs explain significant variation in fitness, but this is no different than saying shape and fitness are correlated, so PLS seems a bit more straightforward, as a result.

The function, shape.predictor, will allow to predict such shapes, whether PLS or fitted values from a linear model are used.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.author: 2fc03d53bc863e8d
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Natural selection analisys using Geometrics Morphometrics
parts: The problem is to find a citable source that addresses this in highly general terms. Even when the geometric argument is highly general, its generality may not be evident to anyone who does not already grasp the point.  The two papers cited by Dean are criticisms of our work, but rather than seeing those papers as addressing a highly general point, people read them as if they were solely about partial warps and cladistics.  Our mistake was failing to realize that you should not analyze data within a Euclidean space by projecting them onto axes of a coordinate system then analyzing each projection, one at a time. There are probably many ways to say why not to do that, starting with the Pythagorean Theorem, but I haven't found one that makes the point with sufficient generality that it can be cited in any context. I think that we need that argument, paired with one that addresses the opposite problem, multivariate analyses of incommensurate data, which treat that space as if it were Euclidean.  The problem of explaining why not to do either is complicated by the perception that principal components are "real", being (for example, in the case of PC1) the "line of least evolutionary resistance" or "the direction of greatest diversification".
